title: Set 9
summary: Earthquake scales, allergies, bees, the suffragettes, monopoly, corporate responsibility, Maslow, class size, copyright and deserts.

items.title: Measuring earthquakes
items.text: You will often hear an earthquake described by its magnitude on the Richter scale, although seismologists now use the moment magnitude scale instead. Either way, the scale is {{logarithmic|linear}}. Each whole number up the scale represents about ten times more ground {{shaking|movement}}, and roughly {{thirty-two|twenty}} times more energy released. So a magnitude seven earthquake is not slightly worse than a magnitude six. It is {{enormously|considerably}} more powerful. The damage it does, however, depends just as much on depth, distance and the {{quality|height}} of local buildings.
items.note: Enormously and considerably both intensify more powerful, and they share a similar rhythm. Shaking and movement both describe the ground, so the page offers no clue.

items.title: The hygiene hypothesis
items.text: In nineteen eighty-nine, the epidemiologist David Strachan noticed that children with many older siblings were {{less|more}} likely to develop hay fever. He suggested that early exposure to infections might help to {{train|weaken}} the immune system. This became known as the hygiene hypothesis. The name is now thought to be {{misleading|unfortunate}}, because the evidence does not suggest that washing our hands causes allergies. Researchers today prefer to talk about old friends: the {{microbes|parasites}} we evolved alongside, in soil, on animals and in our gut, which seem to teach the immune system {{tolerance|resistance}}.
items.note: Less and more are both one short syllable, and without knowing the finding a reader accepts either. Tolerance and resistance are opposite ideas that both sound medical.

items.title: Bees and pollination
items.text: Around three quarters of the world's leading food crops benefit, at least in part, from animal pollination, and bees are the most important pollinators of all. When a bee visits a flower to collect nectar, pollen sticks to the {{hairs|legs}} on its body and is carried to the next flower of the same species. Honeybees get most of the attention, but {{wild|native}} bees, such as bumblebees and solitary bees, often pollinate some crops more {{efficiently|cheaply}}. Their numbers have {{declined|fluctuated}} in many regions, and the main causes appear to be habitat loss, pesticides and {{disease|drought}}.
items.note: Wild and native mean nearly the same thing for bees, so only the sound tells them apart. Hairs and legs are both short, and both are places pollen could stick.

items.title: The suffragettes
items.text: The word suffragette was first used by a British newspaper, the Daily Mail, in nineteen oh six, as a {{mocking|friendly}} label for women campaigning for the vote. The women adopted it with pride. Led by Emmeline Pankhurst, the Women's Social and Political Union believed that decades of polite petitions had {{achieved|changed}} very little, and it turned to direct action: smashing windows, {{chaining|gluing}} themselves to railings and going on hunger strike in prison. In nineteen eighteen, some women over the age of {{thirty|twenty-one}} were finally given the vote, and full equality with men followed ten years later.
items.note: Thirty and twenty-one are both real voting ages from that period, so a reader cannot rule either out. Achieved and changed fit very little equally well.

items.title: Monopoly
items.text: A monopoly exists when a single firm is the only supplier of a product that has no close {{substitutes|competitors}}. Because customers have nowhere else to go, a monopolist can charge {{higher|lower}} prices and produce less than a competitive market would. Some monopolies are {{natural|temporary}}. It would make little sense to build two sets of water pipes to every house, so one firm supplies the whole area, and governments usually {{regulate|subsidise}} its prices. Others arise from patents, which give an inventor exclusive rights for a {{limited|fixed}} period in return for publishing the invention.
items.note: Limited and fixed both describe the length of a patent, and it comes at the end. Substitutes and competitors are both things a monopoly lacks.

items.title: Corporate social responsibility
items.text: Corporate social responsibility is the idea that a company should consider its effects on employees, communities and the environment, not only on its {{shareholders|customers}}. In nineteen seventy, the economist Milton Friedman famously argued the opposite: that the social responsibility of business is to {{increase|protect}} its profits, within the rules of the game. Supporters of the idea reply that {{ethical|careful}} behaviour can be good business anyway, by building trust and attracting staff. Critics worry about greenwashing, where a firm spends more on {{advertising|measuring}} its good deeds than on actually doing them.
items.note: Shareholders and customers both belong in a list of who a company answers to, so the first swap is easy to miss. Increase and protect both suit profits.

items.title: Maslow's hierarchy of needs
items.text: In nineteen forty-three, the psychologist Abraham Maslow proposed that human needs are arranged in a hierarchy. At the base are {{physiological|practical}} needs such as food, water and sleep. Above them come safety, then love and belonging, then {{esteem|respect}}. At the top is self-actualisation: becoming the most complete version of yourself. The idea is that higher needs only become {{motivating|important}} once lower ones are reasonably {{satisfied|understood}}. Interestingly, Maslow himself never drew the famous pyramid; it was popularised later by {{management|psychology}} writers.
items.note: Esteem and respect mean nearly the same and both have two syllables, but the stress falls on different sounds. Motivating and important both fit the claim about higher needs.

items.title: Does class size matter?
items.text: Reducing class size is one of the most popular education policies, and also one of the most {{expensive|debated}}. The best-known evidence comes from an experiment in Tennessee in the nineteen eighties, called Project STAR, in which children were {{randomly|carefully}} assigned to small or regular classes. Pupils in the small classes, of around thirteen to seventeen, did better, and the benefits were {{largest|smallest}} for disadvantaged children. Yet other studies find much weaker effects, and many economists argue that the same money might achieve more if it were spent on {{training|hiring}} better teachers.
items.note: Largest and smallest are opposites with the same ending, so the first sound decides it. Randomly and carefully both describe how an experiment assigns pupils.

items.title: Copyright
items.text: Copyright protects the {{expression|meaning}} of an idea, not the idea itself. You can write your own story about a boy wizard at a magic school, but you cannot copy someone else's {{sentences|characters}}. In most countries, protection arises {{automatically|immediately}} when a work is created; there is no need to register it. Under the Berne Convention, it lasts at least fifty years after the author's death, and in the United Kingdom and the European Union the term is {{seventy|sixty}} years. Exceptions such as fair dealing allow limited copying for criticism, research and {{teaching|reporting}}.
items.note: Automatically and immediately both describe protection with no paperwork, and both are long words ending in ly. Seventy and sixty are both believable terms, so the number has to be heard.

items.title: What makes a desert
items.text: When people picture a desert, they usually imagine sand dunes and blazing heat. But geographers define a desert by its {{dryness|climate}}: an area that receives less than about two hundred and fifty millimetres of rain or snow a year. By that definition, the largest desert on Earth is Antarctica, a {{frozen|barren}} continent where very little snow ever falls. Even in hot deserts, sand covers only a {{fraction|majority}} of the surface; most of it is bare rock and gravel. And because dry air holds little heat, temperatures {{plummet|change}} at night.
items.note: Frozen and barren both describe Antarctica, so reading cannot find it. Fraction and majority are opposites, but the following clause is easy to skim past.
